decks.title: Shares and Dividends — Part 1: Shares, dividend and income
goals: Use the terms face value, market value, premium, discount and dividend
Find the market value of a share quoted at a premium or a discount
Find the number of shares bought for an investment
Calculate the dividend on one share and the annual income

slides.heading: Shares and Dividends, Part 1
slides.body_md: Own a small part of a company and share its profit.

nodes.label: A company divides its capital into shares
Each share has a face value printed on it
Shares are bought and sold at the market value
The company pays a dividend on the face value

visual.alt: Flow chart: a company divides its capital into shares; each share has a face value; shares are traded at the market value; the company pays a dividend as a percentage of the face value.
visual.caption: Two values for every share: face value and market value.

slides.narration: Welcome to shares and dividends. When a company needs money, it divides its capital into many small parts called shares. People who buy shares own a little of the company, and each year the company may share its profit with them as a dividend. In this part we learn the language of shares and work out the income they bring.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the market value from a quote
Find the **number of shares** bought for a sum of money
Find the **dividend** on one share and the **annual income**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. Every share has two values, and most mistakes in this chapter come from mixing them up. By the end you will know which value to use for the price and which to use for the dividend.

slides.heading: Two values for every share
slides.body_md: The **face value** (nominal value) is printed on the share and never changes. The **market value** is today's price.

rows: the value printed on the share; fixed
the price at which the share is bought or sold today
the part of the profit paid on each share, as a per cent of the FV
money spent buying shares $=$ number of shares $\times$ MV
total dividend received in a year

visual.alt: Table of terms: face or nominal value printed on the share; market value, the price today; dividend, paid as a per cent of the face value; investment, number of shares times market value; annual income, the total dividend for a year.
visual.caption: The language of shares.

slides.narration: Every share has a face value, also called the nominal value. It is printed on the share certificate and stays fixed. The market value is the price at which the share is bought and sold today, and it changes with demand. The dividend is always a percentage of the face value. The investment is the money spent at the market value.

slides.heading: At par, at a premium, at a discount
slides.body_md: Compare the market value with the face value:

visual.alt: Table for a ten rupee share: at a market value of 10 rupees it is at par; at 14 rupees it is at a premium of 4 rupees, 40 per cent; at 8 rupees it is at a discount of 2 rupees, 20 per cent.
visual.caption: Premium and discount per cent are taken on the face value.

slides.narration: If the market value equals the face value, the share is at par. If it is higher, the share is at a premium; if lower, at a discount. A ten rupee share selling at fourteen rupees is at a premium of four rupees, which is forty per cent of the face value. At eight rupees, it is at a discount of two rupees, or twenty per cent.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a quote
slides.body_md: Find the market value of: (a) a ₹100 share at a 15% premium (b) a ₹50 share at ₹6 discount (c) a ₹25 share at a 20% discount.
bullets: **Tip —** A per cent premium or discount is a per cent of the face value.

visual.alt: Working table: a 100 rupee share at a 15 per cent premium costs 115 rupees; a 50 rupee share at a 6 rupee discount costs 44 rupees; a 25 rupee share at a 20 per cent discount costs 20 rupees.
visual.caption: Read the quote carefully: rupees or per cent?

slides.narration: For part a, fifteen per cent of one hundred is fifteen, so the market value is one hundred and fifteen rupees. For part b, the discount is given in rupees, so simply subtract: forty four rupees. For part c, twenty per cent of twenty five is five, so the share sells for twenty rupees. Always check whether the quote is in rupees or as a per cent.

slides.heading: Quick check: par, premium or discount?
slides.body_md: Compare the market value with the face value.
slides.narration: Is the market price above, equal to or below the printed value?

slides.heading: Dividend is paid on the face value
slides.body_md: A company declares a dividend of $r\%$. Each share earns $r\%$ of its **face value**, whatever its price:

nodes.label: Annual income $=$ number of shares $\times$ dividend on one share

visual.alt: Flow: the face value times the rate of dividend gives the dividend on one share; times the number of shares gives the annual income.
visual.caption: The market value plays no part in the dividend.

slides.narration: This is the most important rule in the chapter. The dividend is a percentage of the face value, never of the market value. So a ten rupee share paying twelve per cent earns one rupee twenty paise, whether you paid eight rupees or twenty for it. Multiply the dividend on one share by the number of shares to get the annual income.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dividend and income
slides.body_md: Meena holds 450 shares of ₹10 each in the imagined Sahyadri Textiles Ltd, which declares an 18% dividend. Find her annual income.

visual.alt: Working table: 450 shares of 10 rupees paying 18 per cent; the dividend on one share is 1 rupee 80 paise and the annual income is 810 rupees.
visual.caption: Income ₹810.

slides.narration: First, the dividend on one share: eighteen per cent of ten rupees is one rupee eighty paise. Then multiply by four hundred and fifty shares. Meena receives eight hundred and ten rupees a year. Notice that we did not need the market value at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: dividend on one share
slides.body_md: Use the face value, not the price.
slides.narration: Take the rate of dividend as a percentage of the face value of one share.

slides.heading: Buying shares: how many?
slides.body_md: Shares are bought at the **market value**, and only whole shares can be bought:

visual.alt: Flow: divide the investment by the market value to get the number of shares, then find the income from the face value and the rate of dividend.
visual.caption: Buy at the market value; earn on the face value.

slides.narration: When you buy shares, you pay the market value for each one. So the number of shares is the money invested divided by the market value. Turn it around and the investment is the number of shares times the market value. In this chapter every problem gives a whole number of shares.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: shares at a premium
slides.body_md: Arjun invests ₹15,600 in ₹100 shares of the imagined Coromandel Chemicals Ltd at a premium of ₹30. The dividend is 9%. Find his annual income.

visual.alt: Working table: market value 130 rupees; 15600 divided by 130 gives 120 shares; each earns 9 rupees, so the income is 1080 rupees.
visual.caption: Income ₹1,080.

slides.narration: The premium is thirty rupees, so each share costs one hundred and thirty. Dividing fifteen thousand six hundred by one hundred and thirty gives one hundred and twenty shares. Each share earns nine per cent of one hundred, which is nine rupees. So Arjun receives one thousand and eighty rupees a year.

slides.heading: Quick check: number of shares
slides.body_md: Divide by the price paid.
slides.narration: Which value do you divide the money by: the face value or the market value?

slides.heading: Worked example 4: shares at a discount
slides.body_md: Sara invests ₹22,500 in ₹50 shares of the imagined Coromandel Chemicals Ltd at a 10% discount, paying 7.5%. Find her income.

visual.alt: Working table: market value 45 rupees; 500 shares; each earns 3 rupees 75 paise, so the income is 1875 rupees.
visual.caption: Income ₹1,875.

slides.narration: Ten per cent of fifty is five, so the shares cost forty five rupees each. Twenty two thousand five hundred divided by forty five is five hundred shares. Seven and a half per cent of fifty rupees is three rupees seventy five paise. Five hundred times that is one thousand eight hundred and seventy five rupees.

slides.heading: Income grows with the number of shares
slides.body_md: For ₹100 shares paying 9%, every share adds ₹9 to the income, at any price.

visual.alt: Graph of annual income against the number of 100 rupee shares held: a straight line for a 9 per cent dividend through 450 rupees at 50 shares, 1080 at 120 and 1800 at 200, and a steeper line for 12 per cent through 1440 rupees at 120 shares.
visual.caption: Income is proportional to the number of shares; the price paid does not change it.

slides.narration: The graph shows annual income against the number of shares held. Each hundred rupee share paying nine per cent adds nine rupees, so the graph is a straight line through the origin. A higher rate of dividend gives a steeper line. The market value does not appear: it changes how much you pay, not what you earn.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: working back from the income
slides.body_md: How many ₹20 shares of the imagined Coromandel Chemicals Ltd, paying 15%, give an income of ₹2,400? What do they cost at ₹32 each?

visual.alt: Working table: each 20 rupee share earns 3 rupees; 2400 divided by 3 gives 800 shares; at 32 rupees each the investment is 25600 rupees.
visual.caption: Work backwards from the income.

slides.narration: Work backwards. Each twenty rupee share earns fifteen per cent, which is three rupees. To earn two thousand four hundred rupees you need two thousand four hundred divided by three, that is eight hundred shares. At thirty two rupees each, they cost twenty five thousand six hundred rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Which value is the dividend worked out on?
slides.narration: Decide whether the statement is true or false, and say why.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Face value is fixed; market value is today's price
Premium: MV above FV; discount: MV below FV
Income $=$ shares $\times$ dividend on one share

visual.alt: Summary table: market value is face value plus premium or minus discount; dividend on one share is face value times r over 100; number of shares is investment over market value; annual income is number of shares times face value times r over 100.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Every share has a fixed face value and a changing market value. You buy at the market value, so divide the investment by it to count the shares. The dividend is a percentage of the face value, and the income is the number of shares times the dividend on one share.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Number of shares and income (3 marks):** MV 1 + number of shares 1 + income 1
**State** which value you use: MV for buying, FV for dividend
**Mistake:** dividend as a per cent of the market value
**Mistake:** dividing the investment by the face value
**Mistake:** a per cent premium taken on the market value
slides.narration: In the exam, write the market value first, then the number of shares, then the income. Each line usually earns a mark. Watch for three traps: working out the dividend on the market value, dividing the investment by the face value, and taking a per cent premium on the wrong value.

decks.title: Shares and Dividends — Part 2: Return, comparison and reinvesting
goals: Calculate the percentage return on an investment in shares
Compare two share investments by their returns
Find the price or the rate of dividend for a given return
Solve problems where shares are sold and the money reinvested

slides.heading: Shares and Dividends, Part 2
slides.body_md: Is a higher dividend always the better buy?

nodes.label: Earn dividend on the face value

visual.alt: Flow: buy shares at the market value, earn dividend on the face value, measure the return as income over investment times 100, then decide whether to sell and reinvest.
visual.caption: From buying to reinvesting.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. A high rate of dividend looks attractive, but if the share is expensive the money invested earns less. In this part we measure the return on the money invested, compare investments fairly, and follow an investor who sells one set of shares and buys another.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **percentage return** on an investment
Find the **price** or the **rate** for a given return
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. Everything rests on one idea: the return is the income as a percentage of the money invested. Once you can find it, comparing, working backwards and reinvesting all follow.

slides.heading: Rate of return
slides.body_md: The **return** is the yearly income as a per cent of the money invested. It can be found from one share:

visual.alt: Flow: the return per cent is the dividend on one share divided by the market value of one share, times 100; it equals the total income over the total investment times 100.
visual.caption: One share tells you the return on the whole investment.

slides.narration: The rate of dividend is a percentage of the face value. The return, also called the yield, is a percentage of the money you actually paid. Divide the income by the investment and multiply by one hundred. Because every share is the same, you get the same answer from one share: its dividend divided by its market value, times one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: return by two routes
slides.body_md: Kabir invests ₹20,000 in ₹100 shares of the imagined Coromandel Chemicals Ltd at ₹125, paying 10%. Find his percentage return.

visual.alt: Table showing the return by two routes: 1600 rupees of income on 20000 rupees invested is 8 per cent; 10 rupees of dividend on a 125 rupee share is also 8 per cent.
visual.caption: Both routes give $8\%$.

slides.narration: Twenty thousand rupees buys one hundred and sixty shares at one hundred and twenty five. Each earns ten rupees, so the income is one thousand six hundred. As a percentage of twenty thousand, that is eight per cent. The quick check with one share agrees: ten rupees on one hundred and twenty five is eight per cent.

slides.heading: Price and return
slides.body_md: For ₹100 shares paying 12%, a higher price means a lower return:

visual.alt: Graph of the percentage return on a 100 rupee share paying 12 per cent against its market value: a falling curve through 15 per cent at 80 rupees, 12 per cent at par, 10 per cent at 120 rupees and 8 per cent at 150 rupees.
visual.caption: Above par the return is below $12\%$; below par it is above.

slides.narration: This graph follows one share paying twelve per cent on a face value of one hundred. Bought at par, it returns exactly twelve per cent. Bought at a premium, say one hundred and fifty, it returns only eight. Bought at a discount, say eighty, it returns fifteen. So a premium lowers the return and a discount raises it.

slides.heading: Quick check: percentage return
slides.body_md: Dividend on one share over its price.
slides.narration: Find the dividend on one share from the face value, then divide by the price paid.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which is better?
slides.body_md: Compare: A, ₹10 shares at ₹16 paying 12%; B, ₹100 shares at ₹160 paying 13% (both imagined companies).
bullets: **Answer —** B is the better investment: it returns more on every rupee invested.

visual.alt: Comparison table: company A, 10 rupee shares at 16 rupees paying 12 per cent, returns 7.5 per cent; company B, 100 rupee shares at 160 rupees paying 13 per cent, returns 8.125 per cent.
visual.caption: B is the better investment.

slides.narration: To compare, find the return on each. Company A earns one rupee twenty on a sixteen rupee share, which is seven and a half per cent. Company B earns thirteen rupees on one hundred and sixty, which is eight point one two five per cent. B gives more on every rupee invested, so B is better.

slides.heading: Quick check: compare two shares
slides.body_md: Compare returns, not rates of dividend.
slides.narration: Work out the return on each share and choose the larger.

slides.heading: Working backwards
slides.body_md: The return formula can be read backwards for the price or the rate:

visual.alt: Decision chart: the return equals face value times rate over market value; rearrange for the market value or for the rate, then check by working forwards.
visual.caption: One formula, read three ways.

slides.narration: Sometimes the return is given and something else is unknown. If the price is unknown, divide the dividend on one share by the return and multiply by one hundred. If the rate of dividend is unknown, find what each share must earn at the given price, then express that as a percentage of the face value.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: price and rate for a return
slides.body_md: (a) At what price do ₹100 shares paying 9% return 7.2%? (b) What rate must ₹10 shares at ₹15 pay to return 8%?
bullets: **(a) —** $\text{Dividend on one share} = 100 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 9$. For a return of $7.2\%$: $\dfrac{9}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 7.2$, so $\text{MV} = \dfrac{9 \times 100}{7.2} = 125$.
**(b) —** Return $8\%$ on ₹$15$ means a dividend of $15 \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1.20$ on each share. So $10 \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 1.20$, giving $r = \dfrac{1.20 \times 100}{10} = 12$.

visual.alt: Table of two inverse problems: a 100 rupee share paying 9 per cent gives 7.2 per cent at a price of 125 rupees; a 10 rupee share at 15 rupees giving 8 per cent must pay a 12 per cent dividend.
visual.caption: Find the dividend on one share first.

slides.narration: For part a, each share earns nine rupees. Nine rupees must be seven point two per cent of the price, so the price is nine times one hundred, divided by seven point two, which is one hundred and twenty five. For part b, eight per cent of fifteen rupees is one rupee twenty, and that is twelve per cent of the face value.

slides.heading: Selling and reinvesting
slides.body_md: Sell at the **current** market value; buy the new shares at **their** market value; dividends are on face values.

visual.alt: Flow: old shares times the selling price give the sale proceeds; divided by the new market value they give the new number of shares; their dividend is the new income; subtract the old income for the change.
visual.caption: Selling and reinvesting in five steps.

slides.narration: An investor may sell shares and put the money into another company. Sell at the current price to get the proceeds. Divide the proceeds by the new market value to find the new number of shares. Their dividend is the new income. The change in income is the new income minus the old.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a change in income
slides.body_md: Riya holds 400 ₹10 shares of an imagined company paying 15%. She sells them at ₹18 and buys ₹50 shares of another imagined company at ₹40 paying 12%. Find the change in her income.
bullets: **Step 5 —** Change in income $= 1080 - 600 = 480$: an increase of ₹480.

visual.alt: Working table: old income 600 rupees; sale proceeds 7200 rupees; 180 new shares; new income 1080 rupees; an increase of 480 rupees.
visual.caption: Income rises by ₹480.

slides.narration: Before the sale, four hundred shares earn one rupee fifty each: six hundred rupees. Selling at eighteen gives seven thousand two hundred rupees. That buys one hundred and eighty shares at forty. Each earns twelve per cent of fifty, that is six rupees, so the new income is one thousand and eighty. Her income rises by four hundred and eighty rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: change in income
slides.body_md: Old income, proceeds, new shares, new income.
slides.narration: Follow the five steps: old income, sale proceeds, new shares, new income, and the difference.

slides.heading: Gain on the sale or change in income?
slides.body_md: If Riya had bought her shares at ₹12, two different questions have two different answers:

rows: selling price $-$ buying price, per share

visual.alt: Table contrasting two questions about the same sale: the gain on the sale uses the selling and buying prices, 400 times 6 is 2400 rupees; the change in yearly income uses dividends, 1080 minus 600 is 480 rupees.
visual.caption: Gain and change in income are different questions.

slides.narration: Read the question carefully. The gain on the sale compares the selling price with the buying price: four hundred shares times six rupees is two thousand four hundred. The change in income compares yearly dividends: one thousand and eighty minus six hundred is four hundred and eighty. Do not mix them up.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Does a higher rate of dividend guarantee more income?
slides.narration: Think about the price of the new shares before you decide.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Premium lowers the return; discount raises it
The better investment has the higher return
Sell at the current price; buy at the new price
Change in income $=$ new income $-$ old income

rows: the higher return is the better investment
rearrange the return formula for MV or $r$
proceeds $\div$ new MV; new income $-$ old income

visual.alt: Summary table: return per cent is income over investment times 100, which equals face value times rate over market value; compare returns; rearrange for the market value or the rate; for reinvesting divide the proceeds by the new market value and subtract the incomes.
visual.caption: Part 2 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The return is the income as a percentage of the money invested, and one share is enough to find it. Compare investments by their returns. The same formula, read backwards, gives the price or the rate. When reinvesting, follow the money from the sale to the new shares and compare the incomes.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Return (2–3 marks):** dividend on one share 1 + division by MV 1 + answer with per cent 1
**Comparison (3–4 marks):** both returns 2 + conclusion with reason 1–2
**Reinvesting (4 marks):** old income 1 + proceeds and new shares 1 + new income 1 + change 1
**Mistake:** choosing the higher rate of dividend instead of the higher return
**Mistake:** confusing the gain on a sale with the change in income
slides.narration: For a return, show the dividend on one share and divide by the price. For a comparison, find both returns and state the better one with a reason. A reinvesting question usually has four step marks: old income, proceeds and new shares, new income, and the change. Two traps: picking the higher rate of dividend, and mixing up the gain with the change in income.

notes.title: Shares and Dividends — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Shares and their two values
sections.body_md:
A company divides its capital into **shares**. A shareholder owns part of the company and may receive part of its profit as a **dividend**.

- **Face value (nominal value, FV):** printed on the share; it never changes.
- **Market value (MV):** the price at which the share is bought or sold today; it changes with demand.
- Brokerage and fractional shares are not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus: every problem here buys a whole number of shares and pays no brokerage.

key_terms.definition_md: One of the equal parts into which a company divides its capital.
The value printed on a share (also called the nominal value); dividends are worked out on it.
The price of a share in the market on a given day.

nodes.label: A company divides its capital into shares
Each share has a face value printed on it
Shares are bought and sold at the market value
The company pays a dividend on the face value

visual.alt: Flow chart: a company divides its capital into shares; each share has a face value; shares are traded at the market value; the company pays a dividend as a percentage of the face value.
visual.caption: Two values for every share: face value and market value.

rows: the value printed on the share; fixed
the price at which the share is bought or sold today
the part of the profit paid on each share, as a per cent of the FV
money spent buying shares $=$ number of shares $\times$ MV
total dividend received in a year

visuals.caption: The language of shares.

sections.heading: 2. At par, at a premium, at a discount
sections.body_md:
- MV $=$ FV: the share is **at par**.
- MV $>$ FV: **at a premium**; premium $=$ MV $-$ FV.
- MV $<$ FV: **at a discount**; discount $=$ FV $-$ MV.
- A premium or discount **per cent** is a per cent of the **face value**: a ₹50 share at a 16% premium costs $50 + 8 = 58$.

key_terms.definition_md: The amount by which the market value exceeds the face value.
The amount by which the market value falls short of the face value.
Market value equal to the face value.

visual.alt: Table for a ten rupee share: at a market value of 10 rupees it is at par; at 14 rupees it is at a premium of 4 rupees, 40 per cent; at 8 rupees it is at a discount of 2 rupees, 20 per cent.
visual.caption: Premium and discount per cent are taken on the face value.

visuals.alt: Working table: a 100 rupee share at a 15 per cent premium costs 115 rupees; a 50 rupee share at a 6 rupee discount costs 44 rupees; a 25 rupee share at a 20 per cent discount costs 20 rupees.
visuals.caption: Read the quote carefully: rupees or per cent?

sections.heading: 3. Dividend and annual income
sections.body_md:
The dividend is declared as a rate $r\%$ of the **face value**, whatever price the shareholder paid.

$$\text{Dividend on one share} = \text{FV} \times \frac{r}{100}, \qquad \text{Annual income} = n \times \text{FV} \times \frac{r}{100}.$$

*Example:* 450 shares of ₹10 at 18%: $450 \times 1.80 = 810$. Doubling the number of shares doubles the income; the market value does not affect it.

key_terms.definition_md: The part of the profit a company pays on each share, as a per cent of its face value.
The per cent $r$ of the face value paid as dividend.

nodes.label: Annual income $=$ number of shares $\times$ dividend on one share

visual.alt: Flow: the face value times the rate of dividend gives the dividend on one share; times the number of shares gives the annual income.
visual.caption: The market value plays no part in the dividend.

visuals.alt: Working table: 450 shares of 10 rupees paying 18 per cent; the dividend on one share is 1 rupee 80 paise and the annual income is 810 rupees.
visuals.caption: Income ₹810.

visuals.alt: Graph of annual income against the number of 100 rupee shares held: a straight line for a 9 per cent dividend through 450 rupees at 50 shares, 1080 at 120 and 1800 at 200, and a steeper line for 12 per cent through 1440 rupees at 120 shares.
visuals.caption: Income is proportional to the number of shares; the price paid does not change it.

sections.heading: 4. Investment and number of shares
sections.body_md:
Shares are bought at the **market value**:

$$\text{Number of shares} = \frac{\text{investment}}{\text{MV}}, \qquad \text{investment} = n \times \text{MV}.$$

- *Premium:* ₹15,600 in ₹100 shares at ₹130 buys 120 shares; at 9% the income is ₹1,080.
- *Discount:* ₹22,500 in ₹50 shares at ₹45 buys 500 shares; at 7.5% the income is ₹1,875.
- *Income given:* for ₹2,400 from ₹20 shares paying 15%, divide by the dividend on one share (₹3): 800 shares.

key_terms.definition_md: The money spent buying shares: number of shares $\times$ market value.
The total dividend received in a year.

visual.alt: Flow: divide the investment by the market value to get the number of shares, then find the income from the face value and the rate of dividend.
visual.caption: Buy at the market value; earn on the face value.

visuals.alt: Working table: market value 130 rupees; 15600 divided by 130 gives 120 shares; each earns 9 rupees, so the income is 1080 rupees.
visuals.caption: Income ₹1,080.

visuals.alt: Working table: market value 45 rupees; 500 shares; each earns 3 rupees 75 paise, so the income is 1875 rupees.
visuals.caption: Income ₹1,875.

visuals.alt: Working table: each 20 rupee share earns 3 rupees; 2400 divided by 3 gives 800 shares; at 32 rupees each the investment is 25600 rupees.
visuals.caption: Work backwards from the income.

sections.heading: 5. Rate of return
sections.body_md:
The **return** (yield) is the income as a per cent of the money invested:

$$\text{Return} = \frac{\text{income}}{\text{investment}} \times 100 = \frac{\text{FV} \times r}{\text{MV}}\,\%.$$

- Bought **at par**: return $=$ rate of dividend.
- Bought **at a premium**: return $<$ rate of dividend.
- Bought **at a discount**: return $>$ rate of dividend.

*Example:* ₹100 shares at ₹125 paying 10% return $\dfrac{10}{125} \times 100 = 8\%$.

key_terms.definition_md: Annual income as a percentage of the sum invested; also called the yield.

visual.alt: Graph of the percentage return on a 100 rupee share paying 12 per cent against its market value: a falling curve through 15 per cent at 80 rupees, 12 per cent at par, 10 per cent at 120 rupees and 8 per cent at 150 rupees.
visual.caption: Above par the return is below $12\%$; below par it is above.

sections.heading: 6. Comparing investments and working backwards
sections.body_md:
- The **better investment** is the one with the higher **return**, not the higher rate of dividend: ₹100 shares at ₹160 paying 13% (8.125%) beat ₹10 shares at ₹16 paying 12% (7.5%).
- With the same sum invested, the higher return gives the higher income.
- **Price for a return:** $\text{MV} = \dfrac{\text{FV} \times r}{\text{return}}$; e.g. 9% on ₹100 for 7.2% needs ₹125.
- **Rate for a return:** $r = \dfrac{\text{return} \times \text{MV}}{\text{FV}}$; e.g. ₹10 shares at ₹15 returning 8% pay 12%.

sections.heading: 7. Selling and reinvesting
sections.body_md:
1. Old income $=$ shares $\times$ dividend on one share.
2. Sale proceeds $=$ shares sold $\times$ **selling** price.
3. New shares $=$ proceeds $\div$ **new** market value.
4. New income from the new face value and rate.
5. Change in income $=$ new income $-$ old income.

The **gain or loss** on the sale (selling price $-$ buying price, per share) is a different question from the change in income. A higher rate of dividend does not guarantee a higher income: the new price matters.

New annual income minus old annual income after selling and reinvesting.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Shares and income (3 marks):* market value 1; number of shares 1; income 1.
- *Return or comparison (3–4 marks):* dividend on one share 1; each return 1; conclusion with reason 1.
- *Selling and reinvesting (4 marks):* old income 1; proceeds and new shares 1; new income 1; change 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Working out the dividend on the market value instead of the face value.
2. Dividing the investment by the face value instead of the market value.
3. Taking a per cent premium or discount on the market value.
4. Choosing the share with the higher rate of dividend instead of the higher return.
5. Selling at the old price, or buying the new shares at their face value.
6. Confusing the gain on a sale with the change in annual income.

cards.front_md: What is the **face value** of a share?
cards.back_md: The value printed on the share (the nominal value); it does not change.

cards.front_md: What is the **market value** of a share?
cards.back_md: The price at which it is bought or sold today.

cards.front_md: Share **at par**?
cards.back_md: Market value equal to the face value.

cards.front_md: Share **at a premium**?
cards.back_md: Market value above the face value; premium $=$ MV $-$ FV.

cards.front_md: Share **at a discount**?
cards.back_md: Market value below the face value; discount $=$ FV $-$ MV.

cards.front_md: A premium of 20% is 20% of which value?
cards.back_md: The face value.

cards.front_md: ₹50 share at a 16% premium: market value?
₹10 share at ₹14: quoted how?
cards.back_md: At a premium of ₹4, i.e. 40%.

cards.front_md: Picture: a ₹10 share at ₹8, ₹10, ₹14. Name each.
cards.back_md: Discount; par; premium.

cards.front_md: Dividend is a per cent of…
cards.back_md: the **face value**, never the market value.

cards.front_md: Dividend on one share?
cards.back_md: $\text{FV} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$

cards.front_md: Annual income from $n$ shares?
cards.back_md: $n \times \text{FV} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$

cards.front_md: Number of shares bought?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{investment}}{\text{MV}}$

cards.front_md: Investment for $n$ shares?
cards.back_md: $n \times \text{MV}$

cards.front_md: 450 ₹10 shares at 18%: income?
Two people hold the same shares, bought at different prices. Incomes?
cards.back_md: Equal: the income depends on the number of shares, the FV and the rate.

cards.front_md: Income wanted, FV and rate known: number of shares?
cards.back_md: Income wanted $\div$ dividend on one share.

cards.front_md: Most common mistake with the dividend?
cards.back_md: Taking the rate on the market value.

cards.front_md: Rate of return?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{income}}{\text{investment}} \times 100 = \dfrac{\text{FV} \times r}{\text{MV}}$

cards.front_md: Bought at a premium: return compared with the rate of dividend?
cards.back_md: Less.

cards.front_md: Bought at a discount: return compared with the rate of dividend?
cards.back_md: More.

cards.front_md: ₹100 shares at ₹125 paying 10%: return?
Which of two shares is the better investment?
cards.back_md: The one with the higher **return**, not the higher rate of dividend.

cards.front_md: Price for a given return?
cards.back_md: $\text{MV} = \dfrac{\text{FV} \times r}{\text{return}}$

cards.front_md: Picture: graph of return against market value. Shape?
cards.back_md: A falling curve: the higher the price, the lower the return.

cards.front_md: Selling shares: proceeds?
cards.back_md: Number sold $\times$ selling price.

cards.front_md: Reinvesting: new number of shares?
cards.back_md: Proceeds $\div$ market value of the new shares.

cards.front_md: Change in income after reinvesting?
cards.back_md: New annual income $-$ old annual income.

cards.front_md: Gain on a sale vs change in income?
cards.back_md: Gain uses buying and selling prices; change in income uses dividends.

cards.front_md: Does a higher rate of dividend always mean more income after reinvesting?
cards.back_md: No: the new price may be high enough to give fewer, lower-earning shares.

questions.stem_md: A ₹100 share of the imagined Brahmaputra Tea Ltd is quoted at ₹92 in the market. The share is quoted
questions.solution_md: The market value ₹92 is less than the face value ₹100, so the share is at a discount of ₹8. Option (b) would need a market value above ₹100.

questions.stem_md: A company declares its dividend as a percentage. On which value of each share is that percentage worked out?

options.text_md: the price at which the share is later sold
the market value on the day of purchase

questions.solution_md: Dividend is always a percentage of the face value, whatever price the shareholder paid. Option (c) is the commonest slip.

questions.stem_md: Shares of face value ₹50 in the imagined Malabar Spices Ltd sell at a premium of 16%. One share costs
questions.solution_md: Premium $= \dfrac{16}{100} \times 50 = 8$, so the market value is $50 + 8 = 58$. Option (a) subtracts the premium; (b) is the premium alone; (d) adds 16 rupees.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Shivalik Pharma Ltd has ₹25 shares quoted at ₹30 and pays a dividend of 14%. The dividend on one share is
questions.solution_md: $25 \times \dfrac{14}{100} = 3.50$. Option (a) wrongly takes 14% of the market value ₹30.

questions.stem_md: Nisha spends ₹9,800 on ₹10 shares of the imagined Kaveri Agro Foods Ltd at ₹14 each. How many shares does she get?
questions.solution_md: Number of shares $= \dfrac{9800}{14} = 700$. Option (b) divides by the face value instead of the market value.

questions.stem_md: Varun owns 240 shares of ₹50 each in the imagined Aravalli Cement Ltd, bought at ₹60. The company pays 9% dividend. His annual income is
questions.solution_md: $240 \times 50 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 1080$. Option (c) works out 9% of the market value ₹60 per share.

questions.stem_md: To buy 150 shares of ₹100 each in the imagined Satpura Minerals Ltd, quoted at ₹12 below par, an investor needs
questions.solution_md: Market value $= 100 - 12 = 88$; investment $= 150 \times 88 = 13200$. Option (a) adds the discount; (d) uses the face value.

questions.stem_md: What percentage return does an investor get from ₹100 shares of the imagined Doon Electricals Ltd bought at ₹125, if the dividend is 10%?
questions.solution_md: Each share earns ₹10 on an outlay of ₹125: $\dfrac{10}{125} \times 100 = 8$. Option (b) takes 10% of the market value; (a) forgets that the share cost more than ₹100.

questions.stem_md: When a share is bought at a premium, how does the rate of return on the money invested compare with the rate of dividend?

options.text_md: It is less than the rate of dividend.
It is more than the rate of dividend.
It is equal to the rate of dividend.
It is exactly double the rate of dividend.

questions.solution_md: Return $= r \times \dfrac{\text{FV}}{\text{MV}}$, and $\dfrac{\text{FV}}{\text{MV}} < 1$ when the market value is above the face value.

questions.stem_md: Share A: ₹10 shares at ₹15 paying 12%. Share B: ₹100 shares at ₹125 paying 11% (both imagined companies). Which is the better investment?
questions.solution_md: A: $\dfrac{1.20}{15} \times 100 = 8$. B: $\dfrac{11}{125} \times 100 = 8.8$. Compare returns, not rates of dividend, so B is better; option (a) is the trap.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Konkan Cashew Ltd pays 15% on its ₹50 shares. At what market price would these shares give an investor a 10% return?
questions.solution_md: Dividend per share $= 7.50$; $\dfrac{7.50}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 10$ gives $\text{MV} = 75$. Option (b) is 10% of the face value.

questions.stem_md: After a sale, Hari reinvests ₹12,600 in ₹25 shares of the imagined Pench Paints Ltd quoted at ₹35. The number of shares he buys is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{12600}{35} = 360$. Option (a) divides by the face value ₹25.

questions.stem_md: Rekha holds 200 ₹20 shares of an imagined company paying 10%. She sells them at ₹30 and buys ₹10 shares of another imagined company at ₹12 paying 12%. Her annual income
questions.solution_md: Old income $= 200 \times 2 = 400$. Proceeds $= 6000$ buy $500$ shares earning $1.20$ each, i.e. $600$. Change $= 600 - 400 = 200$, a rise.

questions.stem_md: Shares of ₹20 in the imagined Tapti Textiles Ltd change hands at ₹27. They are quoted at a premium of
questions.solution_md: Premium $= 27 - 20 = 7$, and $\dfrac{7}{20} \times 100 = 35$. Premium per cent is on the face value, not the market value.

questions.stem_md: Two cousins each hold 300 ₹10 shares of the imagined Konark Motors Ltd, which pays 12%. One bought at ₹15 and the other at ₹18. Their annual dividend incomes are

options.text_md: larger for the cousin who paid ₹18
larger for the cousin who paid ₹15

questions.solution_md: Each receives $300 \times 10 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 360$. The price paid changes the investment and the return, not the income.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Thar Salt Works ₹10 shares at ₹12 pay 9%. What rate of dividend must the imagined Sundarban Fisheries Ltd pay on its ₹50 shares at ₹80 to give the same return?
questions.solution_md: First return $= \dfrac{0.90}{12} \times 100 = 7.5$. For the second, each share must earn $80 \times \dfrac{7.5}{100} = 6$, so $50 \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 6$ and $r = 12$. Option (c) scales 9% by $\dfrac{80}{50}$ without allowing for the first share's price.

questions.stem_md: Ananya wants an annual income of ₹1,500 from ₹25 shares of the imagined Mahanadi Power Ltd, which pays 12%. How many shares must she hold?
questions.solution_md: Dividend per share $= 25 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 3$; $\dfrac{1500}{3} = 500$. Option (b) divides by 12 instead of by the dividend per share.

questions.stem_md: Gopal sells some shares he owns in the imagined Palar Leather Ltd. The money he receives from the sale equals

options.text_md: the number of shares sold × the price he originally paid
the number of shares sold × the selling price of one share
the number of shares sold × the face value of one share
the number of shares sold × the dividend on one share

questions.solution_md: Shares are sold at the current market price, so the proceeds are the number sold times the selling price. The face value fixes only the dividend.

questions.stem_md: A ₹100 share of the imagined Godavari Fertilisers Ltd is bought at ₹80 and pays 6%. The percentage return is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{6}{80} \times 100 = 7.5$. A share bought at a discount returns more than its rate of dividend; option (a) multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem_md: Leena bought 250 shares of the imagined Kosi Rail Parts Ltd at ₹36 each and later sold all of them at ₹44 each. Her gain on the sale is
questions.solution_md: Gain per share $= 44 - 36 = 8$, so the total gain is $250 \times 8 = 2000$. Option (a) is the sale proceeds and (b) the cost.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ₹100 share of the imagined Vindhya Steel Ltd quoted at ₹112 is at a 12% premium.

**Reason (R):** When the market value is above the face value, the premium is the excess, and as a per cent it is taken on the face value.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Premium $= 112 - 100 = 12$, which is $12\%$ of ₹100. R is exactly the rule used.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sunil's 400 ₹10 shares of the imagined Nilgiri Dairy Ltd, paying 15%, bring him ₹600 a year.

**Reason (R):** The market price of a share changes from day to day.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the income comes from 400 × ₹1.50; the day-to-day price has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** ₹50 shares of the imagined Chambal Paper Ltd bought at ₹40 and paying 8% give a return of 10%.

**Reason (R):** The dividend on a share is calculated on its market value.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A: dividend $= 4$ per share and $\dfrac{4}{40} \times 100 = 10$, true. R is false: dividend is on the face value.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A share bought below its face value always returns less than its rate of dividend.

**Reason (R):** Return per cent = dividend on one share ÷ market value of one share × 100.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true. By R, a smaller market value gives a larger return, so a share bought at a discount returns **more** than its rate of dividend; e.g. ₹100 at ₹80 paying 6% returns 7.5%. A is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Selling 200 ₹10 shares (12% dividend) at ₹15 and putting all the money into ₹100 shares at ₹125 paying 10% leaves the annual income unchanged.

**Reason (R):** Both shares give the same return of 8% on the ₹3,000 involved.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: First return $= \dfrac{1.20}{15} \times 100 = 8$; second $= \dfrac{10}{125} \times 100 = 8$. The same sum at the same return gives the same income, ₹240, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Imagined Kaziranga Tours ₹10 shares at ₹12.50 paying 10% are a better buy than imagined Sabari Mills ₹100 shares at ₹120 paying 9%.

**Reason (R):** A ₹10 share quoted at ₹12.50 is at a 25% premium.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A: returns are $\dfrac{1}{12.5} \times 100 = 8$ and $\dfrac{9}{120} \times 100 = 7.5$, so A is true. R is true too, but a premium alone does not decide which return is higher.

questions.stem_md: A share is said to be at par when its market value is equal to its face value.
questions.solution_md: At par: market value = face value; above it is a premium, below it a discount.

questions.stem_md: The dividend that a company pays on each of its shares is worked out as a percentage of the share's market value.
questions.solution_md: Dividend is a percentage of the face value. The market value matters only for the cost and the return.

questions.stem_md: If a share is bought at a discount, the percentage return on the money invested is higher than the rate of dividend.
questions.solution_md: Return $= r \times \dfrac{\text{FV}}{\text{MV}}$ and $\dfrac{\text{FV}}{\text{MV}} > 1$ when the share is below par.

questions.stem_md: If an investor doubles the number of shares she holds in one company, her annual dividend from that company doubles too.
questions.solution_md: Income = number of shares × dividend on one share, which is proportional to the number of shares.

questions.stem_md: Selling shares and reinvesting all the money in shares with a higher rate of dividend must increase the annual income.
questions.solution_md: Not always. 300 ₹10 shares paying 12% give ₹360; sold at ₹20, the ₹6,000 buys only 200 ₹10 shares at ₹30, which at 15% give ₹300. The price paid matters.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Kaveri Agro Foods ₹50 shares bought at ₹60 and paying 12% give a return of 12% on the investment.
questions.solution_md: Dividend per share $= 6$; return $= \dfrac{6}{60} \times 100 = 10\%$, not 12%, because the share was bought at a premium.

questions.stem_md: On a ₹20 share of the imagined Deccan Solar Power Ltd, a dividend of 7.5% amounts to ₹___ per share.
A ₹10 share of the imagined Pench Paints Ltd quoted at ₹13 stands at a premium of ₹___.
questions.solution_md: Premium $= 13 - 10 = 3$ rupees per share.

questions.stem_md: When the market value of a share is lower than its face value, the share is said to be quoted at a ___.
questions.solution_md: Below the face value is a discount; above it, a premium; equal, at par.

questions.stem_md: Mohan's ₹15,000 buys ___ shares of face value ₹100 in the imagined Malabar Spices Ltd quoted at ₹125.
Priya earns ₹960 a year in dividends from shares that cost her ₹12,000. Her return on the investment is ___%.
Selling 150 shares of the imagined Sabari Mills Ltd at ₹64 each brings in ₹___.
A ₹100 share of the imagined Vindhya Steel Ltd paying 8% must be bought at ₹___ to give a return of 10%.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{8}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 10$ gives $\text{MV} = 80$.

questions.stem_md: Find the annual income, in rupees, from 650 shares of ₹10 each in the imagined Nilgiri Dairy Ltd, which declares a 13% dividend.
questions.solution_md: $\text{Income} = 650 \times 10 \times \dfrac{13}{100} = 845$. The income is ₹845.

questions.stem_md: Tanvi invests ₹26,400 in ₹100 shares of the imagined Doon Electricals Ltd at ₹110. The dividend is 8%. Find her annual income in rupees.
questions.solution_md:
$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{26400}{110} = 240$.

$\text{Dividend on one share} = 100 \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 8$, so $\text{Income} = 240 \times 100 \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1920$.

Her annual income is ₹1,920.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Shivalik Pharma Ltd pays 16% on its ₹25 shares, which are quoted at ₹40. Find the percentage return to a buyer.
questions.solution_md: $\text{Dividend on one share} = 25 \times \dfrac{16}{100} = 4$; $\text{Return} = \dfrac{4}{40} \times 100\% = 10\%$. As a number of per cent: $\dfrac{4}{40} \times 100 = 10$.

questions.stem_md: Shares of face value ₹50 in the imagined Satpura Minerals Ltd are quoted at a 20% discount. How many can be bought for ₹18,000?
questions.solution_md: $\text{MV} = 50 - \dfrac{20}{100} \times 50 = 40$; $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{18000}{40} = 450$. So 450 shares.

questions.stem_md: Arvind sells his 500 ₹10 shares of the imagined Thar Salt Works (12% dividend) at ₹21 and buys ₹100 shares of the imagined Kosi Rail Parts Ltd at ₹150 paying 9%. By how many rupees does his annual income rise?
questions.solution_md:
$\text{Old income} = 500 \times 10 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 600$.

$\text{Sale proceeds} = 500 \times 21 = 10500$.

$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{10500}{150} = 70$ new shares.

$\text{New income} = 70 \times 100 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 630$.

Change in income $= 630 - 600 = 30$: an increase of ₹30.

questions.stem_md: At what price, in rupees, must ₹100 shares of the imagined Brahmaputra Tea Ltd paying 7% be bought to yield 5.6% on the money invested?
questions.solution_md:
$\text{Dividend on one share} = 100 \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 7$.

For a return of $5.6\%$: $\dfrac{7}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 5.6$, so $\text{MV} = \dfrac{7 \times 100}{5.6} = 125$.

The shares must be bought at ₹125.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Tapti Textiles ₹20 shares are quoted at ₹32 and yield 6.25% to a buyer. What rate of dividend, in per cent, does the company pay?
questions.solution_md:
Return $6.25\%$ on ₹$32$ means a dividend of $32 \times \dfrac{6.25}{100} = 2$ on each share.

So $20 \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 2$, giving $r = \dfrac{2 \times 100}{20} = 10$.

The rate of dividend is 10%.

questions.stem_md: How much money, in rupees, must be invested in ₹10 shares of the imagined Godavari Fertilisers Ltd at ₹18, paying 12%, to obtain an annual income of ₹3,600?
questions.solution_md:
$\text{Dividend on one share} = 10 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 1.20$.

$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{3600}{1.20} = 3000$.

$\text{Investment} = 3000 \times 18 = 54000$.

The investment needed is ₹54,000.

questions.stem_md: State whether each share is at par, at a premium or at a discount, and by how much: (a) a ₹10 share of the imagined Konark Motors Ltd quoted at ₹13.50 (b) a ₹100 share of the imagined Aravalli Cement Ltd quoted at ₹96.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $13.50 > 10$: at a premium of $13.50 - 10 = 3.50$, i.e. ₹3.50 per share.

(b) $96 < 100$: at a discount of $100 - 96 = 4$, i.e. ₹4 per share.

questions.solution_md: Compare the market value with the face value.

questions.stem_md: Kamal holds 360 shares of ₹25 each in the imagined Sundarban Fisheries Ltd, which declares a 6% dividend. Find the dividend on one share and his total dividend.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{Dividend on one share} = 25 \times \dfrac{6}{100} = 1.50$.

$\text{Total dividend} = 360 \times 1.50 = 540$, i.e. ₹540.

questions.solution_md: Dividend is on the face value; multiply by the number of shares.

questions.stem_md: Find the percentage return on ₹50 shares of the imagined Pench Paints Ltd bought at ₹62.50, if the company pays 10%.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{Dividend on one share} = 50 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 5$.

$\text{Return} = \dfrac{5}{62.50} \times 100\% = 8\%$.

questions.solution_md: Return per share = dividend on one share ÷ price paid × 100.

questions.stem_md: Find the cost of 225 shares of ₹20 each in the imagined Chambal Paper Ltd when they are quoted at a premium of 15%.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{MV} = 20 + \dfrac{15}{100} \times 20 = 23$.

$\text{Investment} = 225 \times 23 = 5175$, so the cost is ₹5,175.

questions.solution_md: Add the premium (a per cent of the face value) before multiplying.

questions.stem_md: Divya invests ₹31,500 in ₹50 shares of the imagined Mahanadi Power Ltd quoted at ₹70. The dividend is 14%. Find (a) the number of shares she buys (b) her annual income.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{31500}{70} = 450$.

She buys 450 shares.

(b) $\text{Dividend on one share} = 50 \times \dfrac{14}{100} = 7$, so $\text{Income} = 450 \times 50 \times \dfrac{14}{100} = 3150$.

Her annual income is ₹3,150.

questions.solution_md: Shares from the market value; dividend from the face value.

questions.stem_md: Ramesh puts ₹12,000 into ₹10 shares of the imagined Godavari Fertilisers Ltd selling at ₹8. The company pays 6%. Find his income and the percentage return on his money.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{12000}{8} = 1500$.

$\text{Dividend on one share} = 10 \times \dfrac{6}{100} = 0.60$, so $\text{Income} = 1500 \times 10 \times \dfrac{6}{100} = 900$.

$\text{Return} = \dfrac{900}{12000} \times 100\% = 7.5\%$.

His income is ₹900 and the return is 7.5%, more than 6% because the shares were bought at a discount.

questions.solution_md: Find the number of shares, then the income, then compare the income with the investment.

questions.stem_md: Which is the better investment: ₹100 shares of the imagined Vindhya Steel Ltd at ₹150 paying 12%, or ₹25 shares of the imagined Kaziranga Tours Ltd at ₹40 paying 14%? Give the returns.

answer.model_answer_md:
Vindhya Steel: $\text{Return} = \dfrac{12}{150} \times 100\% = 8\%$.

Kaziranga Tours: $\text{Dividend on one share} = 25 \times \dfrac{14}{100} = 3.50$; $\text{Return} = \dfrac{3.50}{40} \times 100\% = 8.75\%$.

Kaziranga Tours is better: $8.75\%$ against $8\%$.

questions.solution_md: Compare the returns, not the rates of dividend.

questions.stem_md: Bhaskar bought 120 shares of ₹100 each in the imagined Sabari Mills Ltd at ₹105 and sold all of them when the price reached ₹131. Find his cost, the sale proceeds and his gain.
questions.solution_md: Cost and proceeds both use market prices; the face value plays no part.

questions.stem_md: Neha invested ₹14,400 in ₹10 shares of the imagined Konkan Cashew Ltd at ₹16 paying 10%. She says, "My income is 10% of ₹14,400, that is ₹1,440." Explain her mistake and find her correct income.

answer.model_answer_md:
The 10% dividend is paid on the face value of the shares she holds, not on the money she invested. Because each share cost more than its face value, her income is less than 10% of ₹14,400.

$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{14400}{16} = 900$; total face value $= 900 \times 10 = 9000$.

$\text{Income} = 900 \times 10 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 900$. Her income is ₹900, which is ₹540 less than she claimed (a return of $6.25\%$).

questions.solution_md: Count the shares and apply the rate to their face value.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Kosi Rail Parts Ltd ₹20 shares stand at a premium of ₹4 and pay 9%. Sanjay invests ₹19,200. Find (a) the market value of one share (b) the number of shares (c) his annual income (d) his percentage return.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{MV} = 20 + 4 = 24$.

(b) $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{19200}{24} = 800$.

(c) $\text{Dividend on one share} = 20 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 1.80$, so $\text{Income} = 800 \times 20 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 1440$.

(d) $\text{Return} = \dfrac{1440}{19200} \times 100\% = 7.5\%$.

He buys 800 shares, earns ₹1,440 a year and gets a return of 7.5%.

questions.solution_md: Premium is added to the face value to get the price.

questions.stem_md: Fatima has ₹28,800 to invest. She can buy ₹100 shares of the imagined Sabari Mills Ltd at ₹120 paying 10%, or ₹10 shares of the imagined Nilgiri Dairy Ltd at ₹8 paying 7%. Which gives her more income, and by how much?

answer.model_answer_md:
Sabari Mills: $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{28800}{120} = 240$; $\text{Income} = 240 \times 100 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 2400$.

Nilgiri Dairy: $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{28800}{8} = 3600$; $\text{Income} = 3600 \times 10 \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 2520$.

Nilgiri Dairy gives more, by $2520 - 2400 = 120$, i.e. ₹120 a year (returns $8\tfrac{1}{3}\%$ and $8.75\%$).

questions.solution_md: With the same sum invested, the higher income is also the higher return.

questions.stem_md: Asha holds 600 shares of ₹10 each in the imagined Brahmaputra Tea Ltd, which pays 15%. She sells them at ₹16 and invests the proceeds in ₹50 shares of the imagined Aravalli Cement Ltd at ₹60 paying 12%. Find the change in her annual income.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{Old income} = 600 \times 10 \times \dfrac{15}{100} = 900$.

$\text{Sale proceeds} = 600 \times 16 = 9600$.

$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{9600}{60} = 160$ new shares.

$\text{New income} = 160 \times 50 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 960$.

Change in income $= 960 - 900 = 60$: an increase of ₹60.

questions.solution_md: Old income, sale proceeds, new shares, new income: then subtract.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Deccan Solar Power ₹100 shares are quoted at ₹135 and pay 12%. Rahul wants an annual income of ₹2,700. Find the number of shares he must buy and the sum he must invest, and check that the income is right.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{Dividend on one share} = 100 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 12$.

$\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{2700}{12} = 225$.

$\text{Investment} = 225 \times 135 = 30375$.

Check: $\text{Income} = 225 \times 100 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 2700$ ✓.

He must buy 225 shares for ₹30,375.

questions.solution_md: Divide the income wanted by the dividend on one share.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Kaveri Agro Foods ₹50 shares pay 9%. (a) At what price do they give a return of 7.5%? (b) Is that price at a premium or a discount, and by what per cent? (c) How many shares does ₹24,000 buy at that price, and what is the income?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Dividend on one share} = 50 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 4.50$.

For a return of $7.5\%$: $\dfrac{4.50}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 7.5$, so $\text{MV} = \dfrac{4.50 \times 100}{7.5} = 60$.

(b) $60 > 50$: a premium of ₹10, which is $\dfrac{10}{50} \times 100 = 20\%$.

(c) $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{24000}{60} = 400$; $\text{Income} = 400 \times 50 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 1800$, i.e. ₹1,800.

questions.solution_md: Price = dividend on one share × 100 ÷ return wanted.

questions.stem_md: Kunal owns 400 ₹25 shares of the imagined Konark Motors Ltd paying 12%. He sells half of them at ₹30 and puts the money into ₹10 shares of the imagined Doon Electricals Ltd at ₹12 paying 15%. Find his total annual income after the change and the increase.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{Old income} = 400 \times 25 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 1200$.

He sells 200: $\text{Sale proceeds} = 200 \times 30 = 6000$; $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{6000}{12} = 500$ new shares.

From the 200 shares he kept: $\text{Income} = 200 \times 25 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 600$. From the new shares: $\text{Income} = 500 \times 10 \times \dfrac{15}{100} = 750$.

Total $= 600 + 750 = 1350$, so the income rises by $1350 - 1200 = 150$, i.e. ₹150.

questions.solution_md: Keep the income from the shares that were not sold.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined Deccan Solar Power Ltd has ₹100 shares quoted at a premium of ₹25 and declares an 11% dividend. Kiran invests ₹50,000 in them.

(a) Find the number of shares Kiran buys, and the premium as a per cent of the face value.

(b) Find Kiran's annual income and her percentage return.

(c) Next year the price falls. At what market price would a new buyer get a 10% return?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{MV} = 100 + 25 = 125$. $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{50000}{125} = 400$. Premium $= \dfrac{25}{100} \times 100 = 25\%$.

(b) $\text{Income} = 400 \times 100 \times \dfrac{11}{100} = 4400$. $\text{Return} = \dfrac{4400}{50000} \times 100\% = 8.8\%$.

(c) $\text{Dividend on one share} = 100 \times \dfrac{11}{100} = 11$.

For a return of $10\%$: $\dfrac{11}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 10$, so $\text{MV} = \dfrac{11 \times 100}{10} = 110$.

A buyer at ₹110 gets 10%.

questions.solution_md: Number of shares from the market value; income from the face value; return from income over investment.

questions.stem_md:
Pallavi has ₹36,000 to invest in one of two imagined companies.
Company X: ₹50 shares at ₹60, dividend 9%.
Company Y: ₹20 shares at a discount of ₹4, dividend 6.5%.

(a) Find her number of shares and annual income if she chooses X.

(b) Find the same for Y.

(c) Find the percentage return from each, state which is the better investment and by how much more income it gives.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{36000}{60} = 600$; $\text{Income} = 600 \times 50 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 2700$.

(b) $\text{MV} = 20 - 4 = 16$. $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{36000}{16} = 2250$; $\text{Income} = 2250 \times 20 \times \dfrac{6.5}{100} = 2925$.

(c) X: $\text{Return} = \dfrac{2700}{36000} \times 100\% = 7.5\%$. Y: $\text{Return} = \dfrac{2925}{36000} \times 100\% = 8.125\%$.

Y is better, giving $2925 - 2700 = 225$, i.e. ₹225 more a year, although its rate of dividend is lower.

questions.solution_md: Compare by return or by income on the same sum, never by the rate of dividend.

questions.stem_md:
Imran holds 800 shares of ₹10 each in the imagined Thar Salt Works, which pays 12.5%.

(a) Find his annual income from these shares.

(b) He sells all the shares at ₹25 each. Find the sale proceeds and the number of ₹100 shares of the imagined Nilgiri Dairy Ltd, quoted at ₹125, that the proceeds will buy.

(c) Nilgiri Dairy pays 10%. Find the change in Imran's annual income and his percentage return on the new investment.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Income} = 800 \times 10 \times \dfrac{12.5}{100} = 1000$. Annual income ₹1,000.

(b) $\text{Sale proceeds} = 800 \times 25 = 20000$; $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{20000}{125} = 160$.

(c) New income: $\text{Income} = 160 \times 100 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 1600$. Change $= 1600 - 1000 = 600$: an increase of ₹600.

$\text{Return} = \dfrac{1600}{20000} \times 100\% = 8\%$.

questions.solution_md: Sell at the market price; buy at the new market price; dividends on face values.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined Chambal Paper Ltd pays 15% on its ₹20 shares. Seema wants an annual income of ₹1,800 from these shares.

(a) How many shares must she hold?

(b) The shares are quoted at ₹37.50. How much must she invest, and what is her percentage return?

(c) If she waits and buys the same number of shares when the price has fallen to ₹30, how much less does she invest, and what is her return then?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Dividend on one share} = 20 \times \dfrac{15}{100} = 3$; $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{1800}{3} = 600$.

(b) $\text{Investment} = 600 \times 37.50 = 22500$. $\text{Return} = \dfrac{1800}{22500} \times 100\% = 8\%$.

(c) $\text{Investment} = 600 \times 30 = 18000$. She invests $22500 - 18000 = 4500$, i.e. ₹4,500 less. $\text{Return} = \dfrac{1800}{18000} \times 100\% = 10\%$: the same income on a smaller outlay.

questions.solution_md: The income depends only on the number of shares; the price decides the outlay and the return.

questions.stem_md:
Ravi invests ₹30,000 in two imagined companies: part in ₹100 shares of Kaziranga Tours Ltd at ₹125 paying 11%, and the rest in ₹10 shares of Tapti Textiles Ltd at ₹16 paying 12%. His total annual income is ₹2,510.

(a) Find the percentage return from each company.

(b) Taking ₹x as the sum invested in Kaziranga Tours, form an equation and find x.

(c) Find the number of shares he holds in each company and verify the total income.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Kaziranga Tours: $\text{Return} = \dfrac{11}{125} \times 100\% = 8.8\%$. Tapti Textiles: $\text{Return} = \dfrac{1.20}{16} \times 100\% = 7.5\%$.

(b) $\dfrac{8.8}{100}x + \dfrac{7.5}{100}(30000 - x) = 2510$, so $0.088x + 2250 - 0.075x = 2510$, $0.013x = 260$ and $x = 20000$. He invests ₹20,000 in Kaziranga Tours and ₹10,000 in Tapti Textiles.

(c) Kaziranga Tours: $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{20000}{125} = 160$. Tapti Textiles: $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{10000}{16} = 625$.

Check: $160 \times 11 = 1760$ and $625 \times 1.20 = 750$; total $= 1760 + 750 = 2510$ ✓.

questions.solution_md: Each rupee invested earns its company's return; set up one linear equation.

questions.stem_md:
Geeta bought 500 ₹10 shares of the imagined Konark Motors Ltd at ₹16. The company pays 8%.

(a) Find her investment, her annual income and her percentage return.

(b) The price falls and she sells all the shares at ₹12. Find the sale proceeds and her loss.

(c) She invests the proceeds in ₹50 shares of the imagined Malabar Spices Ltd at ₹40 paying 10%. Find the number of shares and the change in her annual income.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Investment} = 500 \times 16 = 8000$; $\text{Income} = 500 \times 10 \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 400$; $\text{Return} = \dfrac{400}{8000} \times 100\% = 5\%$.

(b) $\text{Sale proceeds} = 500 \times 12 = 6000$. Loss $= 8000 - 6000 = 2000$, i.e. ₹2,000.

(c) $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{6000}{40} = 150$; $\text{Income} = 150 \times 50 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 750$.

Change $= 750 - 400 = 350$: her income rises by ₹350 a year, even though she lost ₹2,000 on the sale.

questions.solution_md: A loss on the sale and a rise in income can happen together.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part (all companies imagined).

(a) Sabari Mills ₹100 shares pay 9% and give a buyer a return of 7.5%. Find their market value.

(b) Palar Leather ₹10 shares bought at ₹12 give a return of 10%. Find the rate of dividend.

(c) Uday invests ₹24,000 in each of these two shares at the prices in (a) and (b). Find the number of shares of each and his total annual income.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\text{Dividend on one share} = 100 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 9$.

For a return of $7.5\%$: $\dfrac{9}{\text{MV}} \times 100 = 7.5$, so $\text{MV} = \dfrac{9 \times 100}{7.5} = 120$.

(b) Return $10\%$ on ₹$12$ means a dividend of $12 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 1.20$ on each share.

So $10 \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 1.20$, giving $r = \dfrac{1.20 \times 100}{10} = 12$.

(c) Sabari Mills: $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{24000}{120} = 200$; $\text{Income} = 200 \times 100 \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 1800$.

Palar Leather: $\text{Number of shares} = \dfrac{24000}{12} = 2000$; $\text{Income} = 2000 \times 10 \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 2400$.

Total income $= 1800 + 2400 = 4200$, i.e. ₹4,200 a year.

questions.solution_md: Return = dividend on one share ÷ price × 100, read forwards or backwards.
